Red-spotted Argentina frog (Argenteohyla siemersi) eggs, upon fertilization, develop within jelly-coated masses deposited in shallow water. At a constant temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the incubation period is brief, with rupturing of the gelatinous capsule leading to larval eclosion after approximately 7 days [ab = approximately 7 days]. The resulting yolk-dependent tadpoles rely entirely on endogenous reserves; each newly emerged larva possesses a wet weight at birth of roughly 0.0027 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.0027 grams], a remarkably small mass that reflects the minute egg diameter of roughly 1.73 mm. This modest starting size places the species among the smaller-bodied hylid larvae, a trait that likely constrains early survival in highly seasonal wetlands.

Following the endotrophic, yolk-sac larva phase, the exotrophic transition occurs as the tadpole mouthparts develop and first exogenous feeding commences. The free-swimming larvae feed vigorously on periphyton and suspended organic matter, undergoing the typical amphibian morphological transformation. During this larval period, individuals snout-vent length at metamorphosis (Lj) reaches approximately 1.9 cm . This measurement, recorded at the point of tail resorption and emergence of functional limbs, represents the size at which the froglet transitions to a terrestrial juvenile existence. Achieving this developmental milestone is critical for recruitment into the adult population.

From the post-metamorphic juvenile froglet stage onward, growth trajectories diverge markedly between the sexes. At a stable temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], adult asymptotic size, or ultimate snout-vent length, is attained after several years of somatic development. For females, this upper limit approaches 8.7 cm [Li = 8.7 cm], while among conspecific males the corresponding value is notably smaller at 7.2 cm [Li = 7.2 cm]. In conjunction with this length dimorphism, adults also display pronounced differences in body mass at the maximum size. Females achieve an ultimate wet weight of 34.2 grams [Wwi = 34.2 grams], whereas the largest males typically weigh only 19.9 grams [Wwi = 19.9 grams]. Such a size difference likely arises from selective pressures favoring fecundity in females, which require greater body volume for egg production, while males may optimize mobility and territorial defense.

Sexual maturation in this species follows a defined timetable contingent upon environmental temperature. At 24 °C [T = 24 °C], females require a period of approximately 3 years following metamorphosis [tp = approximately 3 years following metamorphosis] to reach puberty, while males develop more rapidly, requiring only about 2 years [tp = about 2 years]. This divergence in maturation rate is common among anurans and is often linked to the relative costs of gamete production. Furthermore, the species exhibits a relatively slow life history pace, as maximum recorded longevity, or lifespan, reaches approximately 22 years [am = approximately 22 years] under favorable captive conditions maintained at 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. Such an extended adult phase allows multiple reproductive seasons over an individual's lifetime.

Reproductive output in Argenteohyla siemersi is characterized by a single annual breeding bout. Gravid females deposit around 2464 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = around 2464 eggs per clutch] at 24 °C [T = 24 °C], a substantial fecundity that supports population persistence despite high larval mortality. The reproductive frequency is limited to approximately 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 clutch per year], presumably constrained by the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and the availability of suitable spawning habitats following seasonal rains. This combination of a large clutch size and low annual event frequency aligns with a life history strategy emphasizing high per-bout investment. Comparisons with related hylids suggest that the relatively large clutch may be an adaptation to unpredictable pond hydroperiods, ensuring at least some offspring reach metamorphosis before water bodies dry.
